Anklam
AHN-klahm
n. (the Pomeranian Hanseatic town on the Peene, a brick Gothic trading port)
German Anklam, from Slavic Tanglim, a personal name; earlier Tanclim.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Anklam on the Peene in Pomerania received town law in 1264, joined the Hanse, and lived by the grain and herring trade through the lagoon to the Baltic. Its brick churches of St Mary and St Nicholas are of the standard Wendish Gothic kind, and its wealth rose and fell with the navigability of the river and the fortunes of Swedish Pomerania; it was burned in the Thirty Years' War, besieged repeatedly, and bombed in the last war. The dictionary records Anklam among the Hanse towns because the merchant's standing is a biblical theme and the merchant town is a standing illustration of it. The patriarchs are described as men who held their tenancy loosely and died holding it, “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13), and the apostle addresses Christians under exactly that double title, “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11). A trading town makes the lesson concrete, because its prosperity is visibly on loan, and the psalmist's confession fits any port, “for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Psa 39:12). The conclusion the epistle draws is not retreat from commerce but a corrected expectation, “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough with full rights; the Hanse as a league of commercial cities; a staple as a settled mart; a sojourner as a temporary resident; and a pilgrim as a wanderer, one who travels to a distance from home.

expand to see more

BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town, or one who possesses a full right of citizenship.

HANSE, n. A society of merchants; the Hanseatic towns were commercial cities in league for protection of trade.

STAPLE, n. A settled mart or market; a city or town where certain commodities are chiefly taken for sale.

SOJOURNER, n. A temporary resident; a stranger or traveler who dwells in a place for a time.

PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

1Pe 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;"

Psa 39:12 — "Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were."

Heb 13:14 — "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come."

Modern Corruption

Pomeranian Hanse port on the Peene, chartered 1264, grown and ruined by river trade and war.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that settled prosperity is a tenancy. Anklam's wealth depended on a river that silted and a crown that changed hands, and the patriarchs are commended for holding their ground on exactly those terms, “having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them” (Heb 11:13).

The live temptation is to read the pilgrim language as contempt for trade and towns. Peter does not; he writes to tradesmen and calls them “Dearly beloved” (1Pe 2:11) in the same breath as he calls them strangers. The psalmist's own confession is made to God and not against his neighbours, “Hear my prayer, O LORD” (Psa 39:12), and the conclusion is a corrected expectation rather than a withdrawal, “but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parepidemos (G3927), a sojourner, a resident alien; Greek xenos (G3581), a stranger; Hebrew ger (H1616), a sojourner; Greek meno (G3306), to abide, to continue.

expand to see more

Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, a foreigner; “they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth”, Hebrews 11:13.

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a resident alien, a sojourner; “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims”, 1 Peter 2:11.

Hebrew ger (H1616) — a sojourner, a stranger in the land; “for I am a stranger with thee”, Psalm 39:12.

Hebrew toshab (H8453) — a dweller, a temporary resident; “and a sojourner, as all my fathers were”, Psalm 39:12.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain, to continue; “here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14.

Usage

"“they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — the patriarchs' own terms of tenure."

"“I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11) — written to tradesmen, not to hermits."

"“but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) — a corrected expectation, not a retreat."
